title: Geometric transformations
intro: A vertex has coordinates in the object's own coordinate system. The model matrix determines where that vertex ends up when the object is placed in the world.
focus: Construct a 2D or 3D matrix from a description, and trace a vertex through the matrix product.
Rotate about a chosen point. Check the signs, the fixed point and the directions of the axes.
Count scalar multiplications for many vertices, both with and without a precomputed matrix product.

sections.title: Working with points, vectors and bases
sections.html:
A point specifies a position, whereas a vector specifies a displacement. From A=(1,1) to B=(4,5), the vector is v=B−A=(3,4). Use the Pythagorean theorem to find its length: √(3²+4²)=5. The unit vector v/5=(0,6;0,8) points in the same direction and has length one. The zero vector has no unique direction and cannot be normalised.

A dot product adds the products of corresponding components. With the unit vector e=(1,0) along the rightward axis, v·e=3. This is the signed component of v along that axis. For two unit vectors, the dot product gives the cosine of the angle between them: 1 for the same direction, 0 for a right angle and −1 for opposite directions. In a right-handed 3D coordinate system, the cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both input vectors. The order of the inputs determines its sign.

You can read the columns of a matrix as basis vectors. For the basis b₁=(0,1), b₂=(−1,0), the local coordinates (2,3) describe the world-space vector 2b₁+3b₂=(−3,2). If the basis is orthonormal, you can recover the local coordinates by taking dot products with the two basis vectors.

Basic practice · How do you check that a vector is normalised?

Take its dot product with itself.

Show answer

For (0,6;0,8), the calculation gives 0,36 + 0,64 = 1. A squared length of one means that the vector has unit length.

Application · our practice exercise

A triangle has vertices A=(0,0,0), B=(2,0,0), C=(0,3,0). Find a unit normal. What happens if you reverse the vertex order?

Hint

Use (B−A) × (C−A), then divide by its length.

Show answer

The cross product is (0,0,2·3−0·0)=(0,0,6). Normalising gives (0,0,1). If you swap B and C, the normal points down along −z. Collinear vertices would give the zero vector, with no unique surface normal.

sections.title: Points, directions and an extra coordinate
sections.html:
The vector from A to B is the difference B − A. Translate both endpoints by the same amount, and the difference stays the same. In homogeneous coordinates, a 2D point takes the form [x, y, 1]ᵀ and a direction takes the form [u, v, 0]ᵀ. In 3D, insert z before the final coordinate.

Use column vectors. The rows of an affine 2D matrix can be written as [a, b, tₓ], [c, d, tᵧ], [0, 0, 1]. The transformed point has x′ = ax + by + tₓ and y′ = cx + dy + tᵧ. The translation terms disappear when the final coordinate is 0.

Work through the calculation yourself. For the point (2,4) with homogeneous coordinate one, we obtain [20301−1001][241]=[731] The direction (2, 4) is mapped to (4, 4). An affine transformation preserves midpoints, among other properties. General scaling can change both lengths and angles.

A cube with eight distinct vertices has a 4 × 8 vertex matrix, with one homogeneous point per column. Scaling by (2, 3, 4) uses a 4 × 4 matrix with diagonal (2, 3, 4, 1) and zeros elsewhere. A translation matrix has ones on the diagonal and the displacement (tₓ, tᵧ, tz) in the top three entries of the final column. The product M · vertex matrix still has four rows and eight columns. All w-values remain 1 under these affine operations.

You can construct an affine matrix by asking where the origin and the two basis vectors are mapped. The first two columns are the transformed basis vectors. The final column is the image of the origin. This gives you a geometric check on every coefficient.

Basic practice · How do you represent a direction?

Subtract one homogeneous point from another.

Show answer

[4,3,1]ᵀ − [1,2,1]ᵀ = [3,1,0]ᵀ. A final coordinate of zero makes the direction unaffected by translation.

Application · our practice exercise

A transformation maps the origin to (4, −2), the unit vector along x to (0, 2), and the unit vector along y to (−1, 0). Where does the point (3, 1) end up?

Hint

Start at the transformed origin. Then take three steps along the new x-direction and one along the new y-direction.

Show answer

(4, −2) + 3(0, 2) + (−1, 0) = (3, 4). The direction (3, 1) on its own would map to (−1, 6). The difference is exactly the translation.

sections.title: Which operation comes first?
sections.html:
S denotes scaling, R rotation and T translation. With x pointing right and y pointing up, positive rotation is counterclockwise when viewed from positive z towards the origin. Rotation in the xy-plane gives x′ = x cos θ − y sin θ and y′ = x sin θ + y cos θ. At +90°, this becomes (−y, x). In 3D, Rz leaves z unchanged.

Scale (1, 2) by the factors (2, 3), rotate by +90°, and translate by (4, 1). Trace the point: (1, 2) → (2, 6) → (−6, 2) → (−2, 3). The product is M = T R S. The rightmost matrix acts on the point first.

Check the complete matrix: (x, y) → (2x, 3y) → (−3y, 2x) → (4 − 3y, 1 + 2x). Read off the rows of M as [0, −3, 4], [2, 0, 1], [0, 0, 1]. The inverse transformation is S⁻¹ R⁻¹ T⁻¹. Try applying it to the result.

To place an already scaled vertex Q = (4, 3) at the target G = (1, 8), find the displacement G − Q = (−3, 5) and apply it to every vertex. Reflection across the x-axis, by contrast, is scaling by (1, −1). A shear along x, x′ = x + ky, y′ = y, maps (1, 2) to (5, 2) when k = 2.

Compose a model matrix

Start with a column point (1, 2). Scale by (2, 3), rotate counterclockwise by 90°, then translate by (4, 1). Reading the operations from the point outward gives M = TRS. The translation occupies the last column because it multiplies the homogeneous coordinate.

[0-34201001][121]=[-231]

What changes if the input is a direction?

Check your reasoning

Set w = 0. Row one gives −3 × 2 = −6 and row two gives 2 × 1 = 2. Translation disappears, so the direction is (−6, 2).

A matrix acts in the coordinate system in which its input vector is expressed. Translating an object before scaling therefore also scales its displacement from the origin. If the stated transformations are easy to confuse, test their order on the origin.

Basic practice · Which matrix acts first in RS?

Put parentheses around the product that acts directly on the point.

Show answer

(RS)p = R(Sp). S acts first.

Application · our practice exercise

Scale x by 3, then translate by 2 along x. What value does the point with x = 1 have when you use the intended order, and when you reverse it?

Hint

Write the two functions as s(x) and t(x).

Show answer

t(s(1)) = 3 + 2 = 5. s(t(1)) = 3(1 + 2) = 9. With column vectors, the first composition is TS. Its inverse must first subtract 2, then divide by 3.

sections.title: Rotation about a different centre
sections.source: Transformations.pdf § 1.6 and § 1.8, PDF p. 15–17 and 29–36 · CGVIZ_Chapter_3_2022.pdf p. 32–35 and 67–80
sections.html:
A centre of rotation C must stay fixed. Translate C to the origin using T(−C), rotate there, then translate back. The formula for a point is p′=C+R(p−C). The matrix is T(C) R T(−C).

Rotate (5, 3) clockwise about (2, 2). The relative position is (3, 1). At −90°, (x, y) becomes (y, −x), giving (1, −3). Add (2, 2) back to obtain (3, −1). Check that C itself gives zero in the middle step.

For an axis parallel to z, use the same procedure and leave z unchanged. For an arbitrary 3D axis through C, a rotation A can first align the axis with z. The complete product is T(C) A⁻¹ Rz(θ) A T(−C). When rotation follows scaling, use the centre expressed in the coordinate system specified for the rotation step.

Subtract the pivot from every point before rotating. The difference is then a direction measured from the pivot. After rotating, add the pivot back in the same coordinate system. Both the pivot position and the distance to it must be preserved.

Basic practice · Where should the pivot point end up?

Substitute p = C into C + R(p − C).

Show answer

The difference is zero, so the output is C. Any other result reveals an incorrect order or sign.

Application · our practice exercise

Rotate P = (3, 4) about C = (2, 2) by 90° clockwise. Check your answer without applying the matrix again.

Hint

A clockwise quarter-turn maps (u, v) to (v, −u).

Show answer

The difference (1, 2) becomes (2, −1). Add C to obtain (4, 1). The squared distance to C is 1² + 2² = 5 before the rotation and 2² + (−1)² = 5 afterwards.

sections.title: Rotating about an arbitrary axis
sections.html:
An axis in space requires both a point C and a direction n. Choose a local orthonormal basis whose third axis lies along n. With the basis vectors as columns, B maps local coordinates to world coordinates. Bᵀ does the reverse because the axes are orthonormal. To construct the other axes using cross products, choose a helper vector that is not parallel to n.

Translate relative to C, change basis, rotate about local z, change back, and add C. This gives C + B Rz(θ) Bᵀ(p−C). For the world x-axis, you can choose the local basis (world y, world z, world x). With C=(1,1,0), p=(1,2,0), the difference p−C is one unit along local x. A positive quarter-turn gives one unit along local y, which is world +z. The result is (1,1,1).

Basic practice · Why normalise the rotation axis?

Compare n and 3n as geometric axes.

Show answer

Both point along the same axis. Unit length makes the change of basis orthonormal, without scaling space.

Application · our practice exercise

What happens to the point (4,1,0) on the same axis?

Hint

Calculate its components relative to C.

Show answer

The difference is 3n, which is (0,0,3) in the local basis. Rotation about local z leaves it unchanged. The result is (4,1,0) for any angle.

sections.title: One matrix for all the vertices
sections.source: Transformations.pdf § 1.4 and § 1.12, PDF p. 10–12 and 46–47 · CGVIZ_Chapter_3_2022.pdf p. 18–20
sections.html:
Multiplying a dense 4 × 4 matrix by one 4-component vector requires 4 · 4 = 16 scalar multiplications. Forming the product of two dense 4 × 4 matrices requires 4 · 4 · 4 = 64. These counts include multiplications by zeros and ones.

For 20 vertices and two transformations, applying the matrices separately costs 20 · 2 · 16 = 640. Precomputing their product costs 64 + 20 · 16 = 384. The transformation order is identical. Reusing the same product saves 256 multiplications. For N vertices, precomputation pays off when 64 + 16N < 32N, that is, N > 4.

Precomputation has a one-time cost and a saving per vertex. Compare them separately. If a new model matrix is needed for every animation frame, the one-time cost is incurred once per frame.

Basic practice · How many products are needed for one output row?

Count the pairs of components in a dense 4-component vector.

Show answer

One row requires four products. Four rows require 16 in total.

Application · our practice exercise

How many vertices must share two dense 4 × 4 matrices before composing the matrices strictly reduces the number of multiplications?

Hint

Compare 64 + 16n with 32n.

Show answer

64 + 16n < 32n gives n > 4. At four vertices, the counts are equal. At five, the counts are 144 versus 160 multiplications. This calculation assumes dense multiplication, without special treatment of zeros.

question: Scale P = (3, 1) by (2, 1), then rotate it by +90° about C = (2, 0). Find the final point and write the matrix factors in the correct order.
hint: First find the scaled point. Subtract C before rotating.
answer: Scaling gives (6, 1). Relative to C, this is (4, 1). The quarter-turn gives (−1, 4). Add C to obtain (1, 4). The matrix product is T(C) R(+90°) T(−C) S.

terms.homogeneous coordinates: An extra coordinate w makes it possible to express translation as matrix multiplication, among other uses. For w ≠ 0, divide the other coordinates by w to obtain ordinary coordinates.
terms.affine transformation: A mapping p′ = Ap + t. A straight line maps to a line or, in a degenerate case, a point.
terms.centre of rotation: The point about which a 2D rotation takes place. Its position stays fixed.
